title: Networking 101 from Harvard & Stanford MBA Grads
summary: Season 1 finale on 'how to talk to anyone', prompted by a listener mailbag question. The sisters cover talking to senior people and executives, building shared experiences and interests, getting 'exposure therapy' to people unlike you, finding male allies as a woman in the workplace, being aware of how you are perceived as a category, and then dating, banter, harmless gossip, and using statement pieces and memorabilia to start conversations without words.

ideas.idea: Talking to executives gets easier when you remember they are just a person and connect human-to-human with genuine curiosity, not sucking up.
ideas.detail: Cherie struggled at 22 when her self-worth was tied to what she said; repetitions and a mindset shift that even someone five levels above you is just a person made it less scary.

ideas.idea: Get your reps in early by taking on assignments that force you to interview senior people.
ideas.detail: Cherie's Morgan Stanley internship required her to interview technologists and VPs for an internal resource directory, which trained her to talk to senior people and to see that she had something to offer.

ideas.idea: Never go into a coffee chat cold; do the research so you ask 'level 10' questions only that person can answer, not 'level 1' questions you could Google.
ideas.detail: The bare minimum is five minutes on the person's LinkedIn profile, especially when you are the one asking for the chat and for help. Cherie's other podcast, Cherie's Corner, is built on heavy preparation for interviewing industry titans.

ideas.idea: The most powerful way to talk to anyone is to find, or actively create, shared interests and shared experiences.
ideas.detail: Cherie co-organized a three-week Stanford Women's Golf Clinic and a creator club at Stanford; Jean runs an annual retreat in Newport with about 20 HBS girlfriends. Corporate affinity groups and traveling together (a Stanford GSB staple) serve the same purpose.

ideas.idea: Growing up as one of the only Asian kids in a white, affluent Long Island community was painful but taught the sisters to be comfortable with people different from them, a strength you can opt into by leaving your comfort zone.
ideas.detail: Jean contrasts California friends who grew up mostly around Asians and still do not feel fully comfortable talking to white people. Jean's view: the world is the world, and you cannot change it without becoming a person of influence within it; leaning into that discomfort helps your career and widens your worldview.

ideas.idea: Seek out non-work interactions with senior people, like company videos, baking competitions or organizing events, so they see you as a person and not a robotic minion.
ideas.detail: At Goldman Sachs Jean produced the group's SNL-style holiday music video, getting MDs and VPs to lip sync Taylor Swift, and won the annual baking competition with sticky toffee pudding cupcakes. She notes those moments are what she remembers most from Goldman despite being 1 percent of her time.

ideas.idea: Being the organizer of a cross-functional event is a low-stakes way to get known by name across teams.
ideas.detail: Cherie organized a baking competition at LinkedIn twice, drawing engineers, designers and data scientists from sister teams; afterwards people she did not remember would approach her in the micro kitchen as the organizer.

ideas.idea: In male-dominated fields, the number one tip for women is to find male allies who will pull you into conversations and coach you to take the 'jump ball'.
ideas.detail: Cherie's boss Albert back-channeled with her, coached her that an unanswered question in a meeting is a jump ball anyone can grab, and DMed her on Slack mid-meeting to take questions she knew the answer to, sometimes setting up a layup for her.

ideas.idea: To cultivate allies, have coffee with someone you admire, then pull them aside right after a shared meeting and ask for feedback on how you presented and how to have more influence next time.
ideas.detail: Walk out of the meeting room beside them and ask; if they are rushing, say they can jot down three thoughts later. Jean, as a former manager, says she would find such a request thoughtful and receive it well.

ideas.idea: Be aware that you are perceived as a category, not just as yourself; young women get 'ingenue' leeway that later turns into being seen as competition.
ideas.detail: Jean's 'cold hard truth': a workplace version of the Manic Pixie Dream Girl means a fresh grad is not seen as a threat and seniors will give honest feedback, but the same tactics land differently once you are more senior. Whether fair or not, perception is often reality.

ideas.idea: Manage your reputation against the stereotype people hold of you, and surprise them by breaking it in a good way.
ideas.detail: A friend who became one of the youngest partners at a VC firm deliberately wanted a wedding ring to seem older among partners 20-35 years his senior. The hosts note married men with kids get an automatic 'responsible' halo that women do not receive, and may even face the reverse.

ideas.idea: In dating, communication starts with energy: being open to receive and radiating openness brings people to you before a word is spoken.
ideas.detail: Jean noticed that after her energy shifted (and she stopped wearing an engagement ring) people began approaching her in the same places as before. You can read whether someone 'glimmers' before they speak.

ideas.idea: Banter is attractive because humor demonstrates both intelligence and the EQ to know what will land with a specific person; it cannot be faked.
ideas.detail: Leading with jokes also lets you read a person quickly by which references they pick up. If you are not naturally funny, watch comedy to learn what you find funny, and use self-deprecating humor or punch up, never down.

ideas.idea: Harmless gossip and quick inside jokes cut through three layers of small talk and build connection; people who claim to never gossip are hurting their ability to connect.
ideas.detail: Cherie bonded with a gym manager by mentioning a rumor about the gym's CFO, after which they greet each other with 'tea' jokes. A TikTok hack she endorses: make an inside joke with someone right away to befriend them.

ideas.idea: Statement pieces and things bought abroad start conversations without words because they carry a story you are excited to tell.
ideas.detail: Jean wears a Van Gogh-print scarf from a Sydney thrift store as a top and has a $17 vintage leather jacket from a Paris thrift store; when complimented, adding 'I got it in Barcelona' opens the conversation.

ideas.idea: Memorabilia like golf-course hats, school gear, hotel caps and concert merch signal your identity and groups, inviting like-minded people to approach you.
ideas.detail: Cherie owns roughly 50 pieces of Stanford clothing plus Barnard and Columbia gear; wearing it near Palo Alto reliably triggers conversations with alumni. Examples given include Bandon Dunes sweaters, Amangiri hats and a Chamois hat from Palisades Tahoe.
